label: prob:gasull
title: Problem
head: environment

label: main-theorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main-theorem}
There exists an small open region $U$ in the square $(0,1/500)\times (0,1/6)$  such that for each pair $(\mu,e)\in U$ the corresponding polynomial vector field $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ given in \eqref{campo-principal} is Hurwitz on $\mathbb{R}^3$, it has a unique singular point at the origin, which is locally asymptotically stable, and exactly two hyperbolic $2\pi$-periodic orbits
\[
\gamma_1:=\left\{(x,y,z)\in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x^2+y^2=1,\ z=-\frac{1}{10}\right\},
\quad
\gamma_2:=\left\{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3\mid x^2+y^2=4,\ z=-\frac{2}{5}\right\}.
\]
Moreover,  $\gamma_1$ is 
 of saddle type and $\gamma_2$ is locally asymptotically stable.
head: environment

label: propiedades-dinamicas
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{propiedades-dinamicas}
Each polynomial vector field $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ given in \eqref{campo-principal}, with  $0<\mu\leq 588/6575$, has a unique singular point at the origin, which is  locally asymptotically stable, and exactly two hyperbolic $2\pi$-periodic orbits
\[
\gamma_1:=\left\{(x,y,z)\in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x^2+y^2=1,\ z=-\frac{1}{10}\right\},
\quad
\gamma_2:=\left\{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3\mid x^2+y^2=4,\ z=-\frac{2}{5}\right\}.
\]
Moreover,  $\gamma_1$ is of saddle type and $\gamma_2$ is locally asymptotically stable.
head: environment

label: invarianza-de-matriz-jacobiana
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{invarianza-de-matriz-jacobiana}
The characteristic polynomial of the Jacobian matrix $D\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ of the polynomial vector field $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ given in \eqref{campo-principal} is invariant under  rotations around the $z$-axis.
head: environment

label: Hurwitz-en-plano-xz
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Hurwitz-en-plano-xz}
Let $\mu=\mu_0=1/1000$ and $e=e_0=1/10$.  The Jacobian matrix $D\mathbf{F}_{\mu_0,e_0}(x,y,z)$ is Hurwitz for every point $(x,0,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The uniqueness of the origin as singular point and the existence of the two periodic orbits $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, as well as their dynamical properties are proved by Lemma~\ref{propiedades-dinamicas}. Hence, it remains to prove the Hurwitz property of the vector field.

Lemma~\ref{invarianza-de-matriz-jacobiana} implies that it is enough to prove the Hurwitz property  for points of the form $(x,0,z)$.
The characteristic polynomial of $D\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,0,z)$ has the form
$$
P_{\mu,e}(\lambda)=\lambda^3+c_2\lambda^2
+c_1\lambda+c_0,
$$
where
\begin{align*}
c_2&=1+ \mu \left( 6\, \left( x^2-{\frac {125}{63}} \right) ^{2}+{\frac {800\,{z}
^{2}}{21}}-{\frac {18650}{1323}} \right), \\
c_1&=\frac{1}{100}\big( 2ex^2+g(x,z)\big)g(x,z)+\frac{\mu }{21}f_1(x,z)+\frac{5\mu^2}{441}f_2(x,z)f_3(x,z),\\
c_0&=\frac{1}{100}\big(g(x,z)\big)^2+\frac{5\mu^2 }{441}f_3(x,z)f_4(x,z),
\end{align*}
with 
\begin{align*}
g(x,z)&=ex^2+10ez+10,\\
f_1(x,z)&=126x^4-160x^2z-500x^2+800z^2+200,\\
f_2(x,z)&=21x^4-75x^2+80z^2+20,\\
f_3(x,z)&=21x^4-125x^2+400z^2+100,\\
f_4(x,z)&=21x^4-32x^2z-75x^2+80z^2+20.
\end{align*}
We prove the Hurwitz property of $D\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,0,z)$  by proving that $P_{\mu,e}(\lambda)$ is stable by using the Routh--Hurwitz criterion for cubic polynomials, that is, we will prove that $c_2>0, c_1>0, c_0>0,$ and $c_2c_1-c_0>0$. 
In fact, we need only to prove the inequalities 
$$
c_2>0,\ c_0>0, \quad \textrm{and} \quad d:=c_2c_1-c_0>0,
$$ 
because the last one immediately yields $c_1=(d+c_0)/c_2>0$.


\smallskip
A straightforward computation gives
$$
d=c_2c_1-c_0=d_0+\mu\Big(d_1+d_2\mu+d_3\mu^2\Big),
$$
where
\begin{align*}
d_0&=\frac{e}{50}x^2\big(g(x,z)\big)\\
d_1&=\frac{1}{21}\Bigg(400+400ez+
(200e^2+1600)z^2+1600ez^3+800e^2z^4
\\ &\qquad \qquad 
+(80e-1000)x^2
-20e(25e-16)z^2x^2+
(80e^2-1000e-160)zx^2
\\ &\qquad \qquad \quad 
+(6e^2-200e+252)x^4 +320e^2z^3x^2-4e(50e-63)zx^4\\
& \qquad \qquad \qquad 
+150e^2z^2x^4+\frac{252}{5}e^2zx^6-\frac{3}{5}e(25e-84)x^6+\frac{189}{50}e^2x^8\Bigg)\\
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
d_2&=\frac{1}{441}\Bigg(
40000+320000z^2+640000z^4-64000z^3x^2-800000z^2x^2\\ 
&\qquad \qquad \quad
-16000zx^2-200000x^2+201600z^2x^4
+60000zx^4
\\ 
&\qquad \qquad \qquad 
+300400x^4-16800zx^6-
126000x^6+15876x^8\Bigg)\\
d_3&=\frac{10}{9261}\bigg(\Big(63x^4-250x^2+
400z^2+100\Big)f_2(x,z)f_3(x,z)\bigg)
\end{align*}

\medskip
We divide the proof into three steps. In Step 1 we prove that $c_2>0$ for suitable positive values of $\mu$. In Step 2 we prove that $c_0>0$ for suitable positive values of $\mu$ and $e$. Finally, according to the constraints we obtain 
for $\mu$ and $e$ in the first two steps, together with Lemma~\ref{Hurwitz-en-plano-xz}, we prove that $d>0$ for values in an open region $U\subset (0,1/500)\times(0,1/6)$ for which
all the roots of $P_{\mu,e}(\lambda)$ have negative real part.  

\medskip

{\bf Step 1.} The coefficient of $\mu$ in $c_2$ has two critical minima at $(\pm \sqrt{125/63},0)$ of the $xz$-plane, whose global minimum value is $-18650/1323$. Therefore, for $0<\mu<\mu_2^*:=1323/18650$, we get $c_2>0$ for any $(x,z)$.

\medskip
{\bf Step 2.}  The functions $f_3(x,z)$ and $f_4(x,z)$ can be written as
$$
f_3(x,z)=21\, \left( {x}^{2}-{\frac {125}{42}} \right) ^{2}+400\,{z}^{2}-{
\frac {7225}{84}}
$$
and
$$
f_4(x,z)=21\, \left( {x}^{2}-{\frac {16\,z}{21}}-{\frac {25}{14}} \right) ^{2}+
{\frac {1424}{21} \left( z-{\frac {75}{178}} \right) ^{2}}-{\frac {
21005}{356}}
$$
Thus, the global minimum values of $f_3(x,z)$ and $f_4(x,z)$ are $-7225/84$ and $-21005/356$, respectively. From the above expressions we get that  the real algebraic curves $\{f_3(x,z)=0\}$ and  $\{f_4(x,z)=0\}$ both are formed by two disjoint closed connected components (symmetric respect to the $z$-axis). Therefore, we look for rectangles $[x_3^{-},x_3^{+}]\times[z_3^{-},z_3^{+}]$ and $[x_4^{-},x_4^{+}]\times[z_4^{-},z_4^{+}]$ that contain the algebraic curves $\{f_3(x,z)=0\}$ and  $\{f_4(x,z)=0\}$, respectively.

The smallest and largest values of $x$ and $z$ in the semiplane $\{x\geq 0\}$ for the algebraic curves $\{f_3(x,z)=0\}$  are computed by using the real zeros of the resultants
$$
Res(f_3,(f_3)_z,z)=640000(21x^2-20)(x^2-5)
$$
and
$$
Res(f_3,(f_3)_x,x)=441000000(4z^2+1)(1344z^2-289)^2,
$$
respectively. Since $\sqrt{20/21}<\sqrt{5}<5/2$ and $\sqrt{289/1344}<1/2$ we obtain that $\{f_3(x,z)=0\}$ is contained in the closed rectangle $[-5/2,5/2]\times [-1/2,1/2]$. Moreover,  straightforward computations give that $f_3(x,z)$ restricted to such rectangle reaches the maximum value $3825/16$.  Analogously, we can show that $\{f_4(x,z)=0\}$ is contained in the closed rectangle $[-2,2]\times [-3/5,3/2]$ and $f_4(x,z)$ restricted to this rectangle reaches the maximum value $200$. 

From the above, $f_3(x,z)f_4(x,z)>0$  in the exterior of the closed rectangle  $\mathcal{R}:=[-5/2,5/2]\times [-3/5, 3/2]$. Hence, $c_0>0$ in $\mathbb{R}^2 \backslash \mathcal{R}$.
It remains to prove that $c_0>0$ in  $\mathcal{R}$. 

The polynomials $f_3(x,z)$ and $f_4(x,z)$ restricted to the rectangle $\mathcal{R}$ reach the
maximum values $16625/16$ and $41629/80$, respectively (attained at
$(\pm 5/2, 3/2)$ and $(\pm 5/2, -3/5)$). Therefore, $f_3(x,z)f_4(x,z)$ has a
global minimum value, which is greater than
$$
\min\left\{\left(-\frac{7225}{84}\right)\frac{41629}{80},\;
\left(-\frac{21005}{356}\right)\frac{16625}{16}\right\}
=-\frac{349208125}{5696}.
$$
Thus, for
$$
0<\mu<\mu_0^{*}:=\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot 441\cdot 5696}{3\cdot 5\cdot 349208125}}
=\sqrt{\frac{239232}{249434375}}\approx 0.031,
$$
we have
$$
\frac{5\mu^{2}}{441}\,f_3(x,z)\,f_4(x,z)>-\frac{2}{3}.
$$
Since $1/500<\mu_0^{*}<\mu_2^{*}$, this inequality also holds for
every $0<\mu<1/500$.

We now analyse the function $g(x,z)=ex^{2}+10ez+10$. Since $e>0$, $g$ is even in
$x$, non-decreasing in $|x|$ and increasing in $z$. Hence, on the closed rectangle
$\mathcal{R}=[-5/2,5/2]\times[-3/5,3/2]$ it attains its minimum at $(0,-3/5)$, that is,
\[
g(x,z)\ \ge\ g(0,-3/5)=10-6e \qquad\text{for all } (x,z)\in \mathcal{R} .
\]
In particular, if $0<e\le 1/6$, then $g(x,z)\ge 9$ on $\mathcal{R}$, and therefore
\[
\frac{1}{100}\bigl(g(x,z)\bigr)^{2}\ \ge\ \frac{81}{100}\ >\ \frac{2}{3}
\qquad\text{for all } (x,z)\in \mathcal{R} .
\]
Combining this with the previous estimate we obtain $c_0 \geq (81/100)-(2/3)>0$
on $\mathcal{R}$. Therefore,
$c_0>0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ for all $0<\mu<\mu_0^{*}$ and
$0<e\le 1/6$.


\medskip
{\bf Step 3.}
We regard $d=c_2c_1-c_0$ as a polynomial in $(x,z,\mu,e)$ and  $(\mu,e)$ varying over the compact rectangle $\mathcal{R}_2:=[1/2000,3/2000]\times[1/20,3/20]$, which contains
$(\mu_0,e_0)=(1/1000, 1/10)$ in its interior.
 Assign weight $1$ to $x$ and weight $2$ to $z$,
so that each monomial $x^{i}z^{j}$ in $d$ 
has weighted degree $i+2j$, and set $s:=x^{4}+z^{2}$. Thus, the weighted degrees of $d_0$,
$d_1$, $d_2$, and $d_3$ are $4$, $8$, $8$, and $12$, respectively. Hence, the highest weighted degree part of $d$ is
the part of $\mu^{3}d_3$ of weighted degree $12$, namely
$$
D_{12}:=\frac{10\mu^{3}}{9261}\left(63x^{4}+400z^{2}\right)
\left(21x^{4}+80z^{2}\right)
\left(21x^{4}+400z^{2}\right).
$$
Then, we can write
$$
d=D_{12}+R,
$$
where $R$ consists of the remaining monomials in $d$, each of which has degree at most four in $z$ and weighted degree at most 10.


On the one hand, the last three factors of $D_{12}$ are bounded below by $63s$, $21s$,
and $21s$, respectively. Thus, we have
\begin{equation}
    \label{primera-desigualdad}
D_{12}\geq 30\,\mu^3\, s^3\geq 
\bigg(\frac{30}{(2000)^3}\bigg)s^3.
\end{equation}
On the other hand,
Since $s=x^{4}+z^{2}$, $|x|\le s^{1/4}$ and $|z|\le s^{1/2}$. Thus, every monomial of weighted degree $w$ is
bounded by $s^{w/4}$. Hence, from the definition of $R$ we get that 
\begin{equation}
    \label{segunda-desigualdad}
    |R|\leq \sum_{j=0}^4\sum_{i=0}^{10-2j}\big{|}C_{ij}(\mu,e)\big{|}|x|^i|z|^j \leq C s^{5/2}, 
    \quad \mbox{for $s\geq 1$.}
\end{equation}
where $C$ is the maximum over $\mathcal{R}_2$ of the sum of the absolute values of the
coefficients of $R$, which satisfies 
$$
C\geq \big{|}C_{00}(\mu,e)\big{|} =\frac{400\,\mu}{21}+\frac{
40000\,{\mu}^{2}}{441}+\frac{2000000\,{\mu}^{3}}{9261}\geq \frac{353641}{37044000}.
$$

Combining the inequalities \eqref{primera-desigualdad} and \eqref{segunda-desigualdad}, 
for each $(\mu,e)\in \mathcal{R}_2$, we have 
$$
d\ \geq \ s^{5/2}\bigg(\frac{30}{(2000)^{3}}\,s^{1/2}-C\bigg)>0
\qquad\text{whenever }
s>s_0:=\bigg(\frac{(2000)^3 C}{30}\bigg)^{2}
 \geq 1.
$$

On the compact set $K:=\{s\le s_0\}$, the proof of
Lemma~3 gives $\delta:=\min_{K}d(\,\cdot\,;\mu_0,e_0)>0$, and by uniform
continuity of $d$ on $K\times P$ there is an open neighbourhood
$U\subset\operatorname{int} \mathcal{R}_2$ of $(\mu_0,e_0)$ with $d>\delta/2$ on $K\times U$.
Therefore, we have proved that $d>0$ on $\mathbb{R}^{2}\times U$. 


In summary, from Lemma~\ref{invarianza-de-matriz-jacobiana}, Steps 1, 2 and 3, the Routh--Hurwitz criterion shows that $DF_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ is
Hurwitz on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ for every $(\mu,e)\in U$.
head: environment

label: rem-nD-vec-field
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem-nD-vec-field}
For every $n>3$ and $(\mu,e)\in U$, the polynomial vector field
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})
:=\bigl(\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x}),-\mathbf{y}\bigr),
\qquad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3,\quad \mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n-3},
$$
is Hurwitz on $\mathbb{R}^n$, has the origin as its unique singular point,
which is locally asymptotically stable, and has exactly two non-constant hyperbolic 
$2\pi$-periodic orbits, $\widetilde\gamma_i=\gamma_i\times\{0\}$, $i=1,2$.
$\widetilde\gamma_1$ is of saddle type and $\widetilde\gamma_2$ is locally asymptotically stable. Indeed, the Jacobian matrix is block diagonal:
$$
D\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})
=\begin{pmatrix}
D\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x})&0\\
0&-I_{n-3}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Hence, its eigenvalues are those of $D\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x})$ together with
$-1$, repeated $n-3$ times, so it is Hurwitz everywhere. The equation
$\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=0$ forces $\mathbf{y}=0$ and $\mathbf{x}=0$;
the Hurwitz property at the origin implies local asymptotic stability.
Moreover, $\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{y}(0)e^{-t}$, so any periodic solution must satisfy
$\mathbf{y}(t)\equiv 0$. Thus any periodic orbit of $\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$  is a periodic orbit of 
$\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(\mathbf{x})$. 
                                                    
                      
Together with Theorem~\ref{main-theorem}, provides  Hurwitz polynomial vector fields in every
dimension $n\ge3,$ having periodic orbits.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In  cylindrical coordinates the vector field becomes
\[
\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)=\bigg(-\frac{\mu r}{21}\Big(21r^4-125r^2+400z^2+100\Big),1+e\Big(z+\frac{1}{10}r^2\Big), -z-\frac{1}{10}r^2\bigg).
\]
For $r=0$ (the $z$-axis), $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$ has exactly one equilibrium at the origin. For $r> 0$, a singular point of $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$ requires 
$$
21r^4-125r^2+400z^2+100=0
 \quad \mbox{and} \quad
  -z-\frac{1}{10}r^2=0. 
$$
This algebraic system has only two solutions for $r \geq 0 $:
   
                                                        
   
                                              
\begin{equation}
\label{solutions}  
(r_1,z_1)=\Big(1,-\frac{1}{10}\Big)
 \quad \mbox{and} \quad
(r_2,z_2)=\Big(2,-\frac{2}{5}\Big).
\end{equation}
For these two solutions the second component of $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$ becomes $1$. Hence, these two solutions are $2\pi$-periodic orbits of the vector field and they correspond to $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ in the statement of the lemma. Thus, the origin is the unique singular point of 
$\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$. 

The eigenvalues of the Cartesian Jacobian matrix at the origin are  $-1$ and $\ -(100/21)\mu\pm \sqrt{-1}$. Hence, the origin is locally asymptotically stable.

Since the second component of $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$ becomes $1$ at the periodic orbits $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, 
the stability of these two orbits only depends of the eigenvalues of the cylindrical Jacobian matrix of the first and third components of $\mathbf{F}_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$, which is
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
-\frac{5 \mu }{21}\left(21r^4-75r^2+20+80z^2\right) & -\frac{800 \mu}{21} rz\\[0.4pc]
-\frac{r}{5} & -1
\end{pmatrix}
$$
The eigenvalues of this Jacobian matrix at $(r_1,z_1)=(1,-1/10)$ are 
$$
 \frac{83 \mu}{21}-\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\bigg(\frac{83\mu}{21}\bigg)^2+\frac{67\mu}{21}+\frac{1}{4}}>0
 \quad
 \mbox{and}
 \quad
 \frac{83\mu}{21}-\frac{1}{2}-\sqrt{\bigg(\frac{83\mu}{21}\bigg)^2+\frac{67\mu}{21}+\frac{1}{4}}<0.
$$
Hence, the periodic orbit $\gamma_1$  is  hyperbolic of saddle type.


The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix at $(r_2,z_2)=(2,-2/5)$ are   
$$
-\frac{172 \mu}{21}-\frac{1}{2}
+\sqrt{\bigg(\frac{172 \mu}{21}\bigg)^2-\frac{428 \mu}{21}+\frac{1}{4}}
\quad
 \mbox{and}
 \quad
 -\frac{172 \mu}{21}-\frac{1}{2}
-\sqrt{\bigg(\frac{172 \mu}{21}\bigg)^2-\frac{428\mu}{21}+\frac{1}{4}},
$$
whose real part is negative for $0<\mu$.
Hence, the periodic orbit $\gamma_2$  is locally asymptotically stable.

It remains to prove that $F_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ has no periodic orbits other than
$\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$. The restriction of $F_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ to the $z$-axis gives $F_{\mu,e}(0,0,z)=(0,0,-z)$, which implies that the $z$-axis is an invariant straight line of $F_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$. Hence, any periodic orbit of $F_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$ is contained in the complement of the $z$-axis. To look for such periodic orbits, we will use $F_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$, with $r>0$.

Since the first and third components of
$F_{\mu,e}(r,\theta,z)$ do not depend on $\theta$, they define the planar
polynomial vector field
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reduced}
X_{\mu}(r,z):=\left(-\frac{\mu r}{21}\left(21r^{4}-125r^{2}+400z^{2}+100\right),\;
-z-\frac{1}{10}r^{2}\right),
\end{equation}
which we call the reduced vector field. Note that $X_{\mu}(r,z)$ does not depend on
$e$. 
 
Let $\Gamma$ be a $T$-periodic orbit of $F_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$. The projection $(x,y,z)\to(r,z)$ sends $\Gamma$ onto either a singular point, or a periodic orbit or a polycycle (or graphic) of the planar vector field $X_{\mu}(r,z)$, contained in the right half-plane $\mathbb{H}:=\{r>0\}$, which is invariant under the flow of $X_{\mu}(r,z)$. The singular points of
$X_{\mu}(r,z)$ in $\mathbb{H}$ are exactly $(r_1,z_1)$ and $(r_2,z_2)$ in \eqref{solutions}, which correspond to the periodic orbits $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, respectively. This fact and the uniqueness of trajectories of $C^1$ vector fields imply that the projection of $\Gamma$ is not be a polycycle. So, it must be a periodic orbit of $X_{\mu}(r,z)$. We
claim that this case cannot occur. Indeed, a direct computation gives
\begin{equation*}
\label{eq:div}
\operatorname{div}X_{\mu}(r,z)
=-1-\mu\Bigg(5\bigg(r^{2}-\frac{25}{14}\bigg)^{2}+\frac{400}{21}z^{2}
-\frac{6575}{588}\Bigg),
\end{equation*}
whence for $0<\mu\leq 588/6575$, we have
$$
\operatorname{div}X_{\mu}(r,z)\le-1+\frac{6575}{588}\,\mu<0
\qquad\text{for all }(r,z)\in\mathbb{H}.
$$
Since $\mathbb{H}$ is simply connected, the Bendixson criterion implies that $X_{\mu}(r,z)$ does not have (non-constant) periodic orbits in $\mathbb{H}$. This proves the
claim. Therefore, $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are the only two periodic orbits of
$F_{\mu,e}(x,y,z)$, for 
$0< \mu \leq 588/6575$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the rotation matrix  $R_\theta$
that makes a rotation by an angle $\theta\in [0,2\pi]$ around the $z$-axis. Since $x^2+y^2$ is invariant under these rotations, the field satisfies
\[
\mathbf{F}(R_\theta \mathbf{q})=R_\theta \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{q}), \qquad \mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^3.
\]
Differentiating with respect to $\mathbf{q}$, with $\theta$ fixed, yields
\[
D\mathbf{F}(R_\theta \mathbf{q})R_\theta=R_\theta D\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{q}).
\]
Multiplying by the right  this last equation with $R_\theta^{-1}$, we get
\[
D\mathbf{F}(R_\theta \mathbf{q})=R_\theta D\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{q})R_\theta^{-1}.
\]
Therefore, the characteristic polynomials of $D\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{q})$ and $D\mathbf{F}(R_\theta \mathbf{q})$ are the same.
head: environment

label: campo-principal-part
title: Proof
head: environment
